claims.statement: By the middle third millennium BCE cuneiform served economic, religious, political, literary and scholarly domains.
claims.counterevidence: Chronologies differ by genre and city; ‘by’ does not mean simultaneous everywhere.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: Lexical lists form a continuous knowledge-organizing tradition from the earliest writing through later cuneiform cultures.
claims.counterevidence: Continuity involved copying, reordering and transformation, not static preservation.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: Legal documents, letters and contracts provide human-scale cases but are mediated by scribal formula and institutional context.
claims.counterevidence: First-person grammar is not transparent access to private interiority.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: Functional expansion should be narrated as successive additions and recombinations, not a ladder from accounting to literature.
claims.counterevidence: Local discontinuities and corpus gaps remain.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

claims.statement: ETCSL's 394 literary compositions are modern composites based on late-third- and early-second-millennium manuscripts, so they are evidence for textual tradition rather than transparent transcripts of an original speaker.
claims.counterevidence: Individual manuscripts can preserve locally and chronologically specific variants when cited at tablet level.
claims.narrative_implication: Attribute translation and edition; identify composite status and avoid invented authorial interiority.

claims.statement: The bounded primary-text shortlist is fixed to four cases: administrative tablet P005390/MMA 1988.433.2, private letter MMA 86.11.111, lexical school tablet P228744, and literary composition ETCSL 3.1.19.
claims.counterevidence: The four cases cover distinct functional turns but cannot represent every city, period, social group or genre.
claims.narrative_implication: Use only these four handoff candidates unless a later production task documents why a substitution is needed.

claims.statement: Published English translations are editorial products and require attribution and rights review before direct quotation.
claims.counterevidence: Met object images selected here are explicitly Public Domain, but that status does not extend to modern catalogue prose, CDLI/Penn photographs or ETCSL/CTMMA translations.
claims.narrative_implication: Met images may be used with object credit; paraphrase modern translations unless a production-stage rights check clears quotation.

claims.statement: MMA 86.11.111 is a ca. 1632 BCE Old Babylonian letter in which Marduk-mushallim reports failure to implement a royal security order.
claims.counterevidence: Its probable Sippar-Yahrurum origin lacks excavated context, and the museum itself presents the letter as unusual.
claims.narrative_implication: Use as an exceptional human-scale epistolary case illustrating reporting and command, not as representative everyday correspondence or proof that writing caused compliance.

claims.statement: P228744 is a fragmented Old Babylonian lexical school tablet excavated at Nippur and a witness to the OB Nippur Ura 03 composite Q000001.
claims.counterevidence: The obverse is missing and the record does not preserve detailed stratigraphy; formal school material cannot establish population-wide literacy.
claims.narrative_implication: Use as a representative case of formal lexical classification and copying within the Nippur training tradition only.

claims.statement: ETCSL 3.1.19 is a modern composite of the Puzur-Shulgi royal letter tradition assembled from multiple Old Babylonian manuscripts, not a contemporary Ur III dispatch.
claims.counterevidence: Individual witnesses such as 3N-T311/IM 58418 preserve substantial portions and can be cited separately, but no one witness equals the complete ETCSL text.
claims.narrative_implication: Use to show retrospective political/literary memory and scribal copying; always distinguish narrated event, manuscript date and modern reconstruction.

sources.title: Cuneiform tablet: private letter
sources.author: Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.type: primary artifact record with scholarly overview
locators: Overview: Marduk-mushallim's report on non-implementation of a royal security order
Artwork details: Old Babylonian, ca. 1632 BCE, probably Sippar-Yahrurum
limitations: Purchased in 1886; exact archaeological context is unavailable and geography is qualified as probable. The letter is unusual, so it cannot represent ordinary correspondence.
notes: Selected epistolary object. Treat as an ancient documentary letter, not an Old Babylonian school copy. Met object images are marked Public Domain; modern translation wording is not cleared for direct quotation.

sources.title: Letter from Puzur-Shulgi to Ibbi-Suen about Ishbi-Erra's claim on Isin (ETCSL 3.1.19)
sources.author: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, University of Oxford
sources.authority: Curated Sumerian literary corpus with manuscript list and edition bibliography
locators: Cuneiform witnesses include 3N-T311 = IM 58418 and IM 13347; full witness list in bibliography
limitations: The online text is a modern composite reconstructed from multiple Old Babylonian school manuscripts. It is not a surviving contemporary Ur III letter or a single speaker's unmediated voice.
notes: Selected literary-memory text. The narrated setting belongs to the end of Ur III, while the surviving manuscripts are later Old Babylonian copies.
